why_how.text: A quick check before driving catches broken equipment and puts your seat and mirrors where you need them.

scenario.text: Grace gets into a borrowed car for an errand.

reasoning.text: She adjusts the seat, steering wheel and mirrors, starts the car, then checks that the turn signals and brakes work.

result.text: Only after both steps does she put the car in motion.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the brake and signal check belongs before you start the engine.

correction.text: Seat, steering wheel and mirrors are adjusted before starting, while the turn signal and brake check is the step before moving.

prompt.text: You have started the car. What should you check before putting it in motion?

answer.text: That the turn signals and brakes work.

rationale.text: The signal and brake check is the last step before moving, after the seat, wheel and mirrors are set.

narration.text: This lesson begins the section on getting ready to drive. The first rule is about the vehicle itself. Your vehicle may not have defective or missing equipment, and the brakes, speedometer, turn signals, horn and emergency flashers must all be in working order. After that come the parts of the car you can see and touch, and then two short routines: what to adjust before you start the engine, and what to check before you put the car in motion. Getting the order right is the main idea of this lesson, so watch for it. Each item matters on its own.

The equipment list continues. The windshield must be intact, the tires in good condition, the seat belts working, and the driver and front passenger side windows operational. Put this together with the earlier list and you have the full picture: brakes, speedometer, turn signals, horn and emergency flashers working, no missing or defective equipment, an intact windshield, good tires, working seat belts and operational front side windows. Each item is its own requirement. If any one of them is missing or broken, the vehicle does not meet the rule.

Here is the first routine. Before starting the vehicle, adjust your seat, the steering wheel, and the rearview and outside mirrors. These adjustments are about fitting the car to you, so they belong before the engine is running. When the seat, the steering wheel and every mirror are set, you can reach the controls and see around the car before anything else happens. The next routine comes only after the car is started. In other words, the seat, the steering wheel, the rearview mirror and the outside mirrors are all set while the car is still off, so your position is ready before the next routine begins.

Here is the order people mix up. Before putting the vehicle in motion, check that the turn signals and brakes work. The manual places the two routines one after the other. Seat, steering wheel and mirrors are adjusted before you start the vehicle, while the turn signal and brake check is the step before you put it in motion. So the adjustments come first, the engine starts, the signals and brakes are checked, and only then does the car move. Starting the engine sits between the two routines, which is the easiest way to remember where each one belongs.

Here is a quick check: you have adjusted the seat and mirrors and started the car. What should you check before you put it in motion? The answer is that the turn signals and brakes work. Before putting the vehicle in motion, check that the turn signals and brakes work. If you were tempted to say the mirrors, remember that they were adjusted earlier, before starting. Seat, steering wheel and mirrors are adjusted before you start the vehicle, while the turn signal and brake check is the step before you put it in motion. Each routine has its own place in the order.

lines.text: Adjust seat, wheel and mirrors first.
Check signals and brakes before moving.

narration.text: To close, your vehicle may not have defective or missing equipment, and its brakes, speedometer, turn signals, horn and emergency flashers must work. The windshield must be intact, the tires in good condition, the seat belts working and the front side windows operational. Before starting, adjust your seat, the steering wheel and the rearview and outside mirrors. Before moving, check that the turn signals and brakes work. Keep those two routines in that order every time you drive. Both routines come straight from the manual's list of steps before you drive.

why_how.text: Arizona's weather is hard on tires, so regular checks of pressure and tread matter here.

scenario.text: Omar plans a winter drive into the high country.

reasoning.text: He checks his tire pressure against the recommended number on the door jamb and does the penny test in the lowest groove.

result.text: He can see all of Lincoln's head, so it may be time for new tires before the trip.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the penny test tells you whether the tires need air.

correction.text: Pressure is checked with a gauge against the vehicle's recommended number on the door jamb, while the penny test checks tread wear.

memory_support.text: Gauge for air, penny for wear.

prompt.text: During the penny test, no part of Lincoln's head is covered by tread. What does that suggest?

answer.text: It may be time for new tires.

rationale.text: When the tread covers none of Lincoln's head in the lowest groove, the tread is low and new tires may be needed.

narration.text: This lesson is about keeping your tires ready for Arizona roads. Here is why the manual gives tires special attention. Arizona's extremes — intense summer heat, summer monsoon storms, and winter snow and ice in the high country — make tire maintenance especially important. With weather that changes from extreme heat to monsoon storms to snow and ice in the high country, tires work harder here than in milder places. We will cover the best way to have them checked and two checks you can do yourself. Each part of this lesson ties back to that weather.

lines.text: The best way to be sure.

narration.text: The manual names one option above the rest. A free inspection from a tire professional, which many offer, is the best way to make sure your tires can handle Arizona conditions. A professional inspection is the top choice because it covers your tires against the conditions you are likely to face, and many tire professionals offer it free. The two checks in the next slides are ones you can also do on your own between inspections. The manual does not say how often to have the inspection, only that it is the best way to be sure your tires can handle Arizona conditions.

lines.text: Gauge, then add or release air.

narration.text: To check tire pressure, find your vehicle's recommended pressure, which is usually printed on the door jamb. Read each tire with a pressure gauge, then add or release air as needed until it matches. The number on the door jamb is the target, and the gauge tells you how far from it each tire is. This check is about the air inside the tire. Remember the three parts of the routine in order: find the recommended number, measure each tire with the gauge, then add or release air until the reading matches. The recommended number comes from your own vehicle, usually printed on the door jamb.

Here is the trap. People sometimes think one quick check covers everything about a tire. The manual describes two different checks for two different things. Tire pressure is checked against the recommended number on the door jamb with a gauge, while tread depth is checked with the penny test. One is about air, the other is about wear. So treat them as two separate habits: a gauge reading against the door jamb number for air, and a penny placed in the lowest groove for tread wear. Doing one does not replace doing the other.

lines.text: Lincoln's head into a low groove.
It may be time for new tires.

narration.text: Here is the tread check. For the penny test, put Lincoln's head into a groove where the tread looks lowest; if no part of his head is covered by tread, it may be time for new tires. Use the groove that looks lowest, because that is where the wear shows first. If tread covers part of the head, the tire still has some depth. If you can see the whole head, the manual's advice is that it may be time to replace the tires. The penny goes in head first, with Lincoln's head into the groove, and you look at how much of the head the tread covers.

Here is a quick check: you place a penny in the lowest groove, and no part of Lincoln's head is covered by tread. What does that suggest? The answer is that it may be time for new tires. For the penny test, put Lincoln's head into a groove where the tread looks lowest; if no part of his head is covered by tread, it may be time for new tires. If you thought it meant the tires need air, remember that air is checked separately with a gauge against the number on the door jamb. The penny test is about wear, and the gauge is about air.

lines.text: Arizona weather is hard on tires.
Pressure by gauge, tread by penny.

narration.text: To finish, Arizona's summer heat, monsoon storms and high-country snow and ice make tire maintenance especially important, and a free inspection from a tire professional is the best way to be sure your tires are ready. To check pressure, find the recommended number on the door jamb, read the tire with a gauge, and add or release air. For tread, do the penny test in the lowest groove; if no part of Lincoln's head is covered, it may be time for new tires. Use both checks, along with a professional inspection, to keep your tires ready for Arizona roads.

why_how.text: Belts are the main protection in a crash, and Arizona sets clear duties for who must wear them.

scenario.text: Ben drives with his fourteen year old nephew in the back seat and a friend up front.

reasoning.text: His friend must wear the lap and shoulder belt, and Ben must make his nephew buckle up because he is under sixteen.

result.text: Both passengers are belted before Ben drives off.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the driver's buckle-up duty covers only front seat passengers.

correction.text: The front-seat rule covers every front occupant, and the driver's duty covers every passenger under sixteen, wherever they sit.

memory_support.text: Front seat everyone; under sixteen, the driver's job.

prompt.text: A fifteen year old rides in the back seat. Whose job is it to make sure the passenger is buckled?

rationale.text: The driver must make every passenger under sixteen buckle up, separate from the front-seat rule for everyone.

lines.text: Front seat lap and shoulder belts.
The driver's duty for young passengers.

narration.text: This lesson covers safety belts: who must wear them and what they do. Start with the front seat. Every front seat occupant must wear the lap and shoulder belt, properly adjusted and fastened, whenever the vehicle is moving. We will then look at seats that have only a lap belt, the driver's duty for younger passengers, what each part of the belt protects in a crash, and one special case for cars with an automatic shoulder belt. Each rule is short, so learn each one exactly. Every one of these rules applies whenever the vehicle is moving.

lines.text: A lap-only seat still needs its belt.

narration.text: Some seats have only a lap belt. Where only a lap belt is installed at a seat, that lap belt must be properly adjusted and fastened while the vehicle is moving. The same idea appears again in the rule for newer vehicles: each front seat occupant of a motor vehicle made after nineteen seventy-two must have a seat belt fastened and adjusted. So the shape of the belt does not matter. Whatever belt is installed at the seat must be worn properly while the vehicle is moving. A lap belt alone is still a belt, and it has to be worn.

lines.text: The driver makes them buckle up.

narration.text: Here is a duty that belongs to the driver alone. The driver must make every passenger under sixteen buckle up. The manual compares this with the front-seat rule. The front-seat belt rule covers every front seat occupant of any age, while the driver's duty to make passengers buckle up covers every passenger under sixteen. So two rules work together: everyone in front wears a belt, and the driver also makes sure every passenger under sixteen is buckled. A back seat passenger who is fifteen is covered by the driver's duty, even though the front-seat rule does not reach the back seat.

lines.text: The combined belt cuts serious injury.
The shoulder belt protects head and chest.

narration.text: Here is why belts matter. A combined lap and shoulder belt greatly cuts your chance of serious injury in a crash, and the lap belt keeps you from being thrown out of the vehicle. The shoulder belt stops your head and chest from hitting the dashboard or windshield. Together the two parts protect different areas of the body, so wearing only one part leaves the other area exposed. Picture the two parts at work: the lap belt holds your body in the seat so you are not thrown out, and the shoulder belt keeps your head and chest away from the dashboard and windshield. Wearing both parts, adjusted and fastened, gives you the protection the manual describes.

title.text: Do not skip the lap belt

lines.text: Automatic shoulder belt, manual lap belt.

narration.text: Here is a trap in some older cars. When the shoulder belt moves into place by itself, people forget the lap belt. In vehicles with an automatic shoulder belt and a manual lap belt, buckling the lap belt is extremely important. The manual explains the difference between the two parts. The lap belt prevents ejection and protects the lower body, while the shoulder belt protects the head and chest from the dashboard and windshield. So in a car with an automatic shoulder belt, the lap belt is the part you must remember to buckle yourself.

lines.text: A fifteen year old in the back.
Who makes sure of the belt?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a fifteen year old rides in the back seat. Whose job is it to make sure that passenger is buckled? The answer is the driver's. The driver must make every passenger under sixteen buckle up. The front-seat rule would not cover a back seat passenger, but the driver's duty covers every passenger under sixteen, wherever they sit. The front-seat belt rule covers every front seat occupant of any age, while the driver's duty to make passengers buckle up covers every passenger under sixteen. The seat does not change the duty.

lines.text: Lap and shoulder belts each protect.

narration.text: To sum up, every front seat occupant must wear the lap and shoulder belt, properly adjusted and fastened, whenever the vehicle is moving, and a lap-only seat still requires its lap belt. The driver must make every passenger under sixteen buckle up. A combined belt greatly cuts the chance of serious injury, the lap belt keeps you from being thrown out, and the shoulder belt protects your head and chest. With an automatic shoulder belt and a manual lap belt, buckling the lap belt is extremely important. These belt rules apply on every trip.

why_how.text: Seat belts are not designed for children, so Arizona law sets ages and a height for child restraints.
Air bags save adults but are unsafe for young children, which decides where children should sit.

scenario.text: Kara drives her four year old and her seven year old, who is four feet five inches tall.

reasoning.text: The four year old must be in a child restraint, and so must the seven year old, who has not reached four feet nine inches.

result.text: Both children ride in the back seat, because children twelve and under should never ride in front.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a child can move to the front seat once the car seat is no longer required.

correction.text: Car-seat ages stop at eight, but children twelve and under should never ride in front because air bags are unsafe for them.

memory_support.text: Under five always, to eight until four nine, twelve and under in back.

prompt.text: A six year old has reached four feet ten inches. Does Arizona still require a child restraint?

answer.text: No, from five to eight the restraint is required only until the child reaches four feet nine inches.

rationale.text: Under five a restraint is always required, but from five to eight it ends once the child reaches four feet nine inches.

lines.text: Belts are not designed for children.

narration.text: This lesson is about children in the car. Here is the starting point in Arizona law. Seat belts are not designed for children, and Arizona law forbids driving on state highways with a child under five who is not properly secured in a child restraint system. We will build on that with the rule for older children, what to do with several children, the standards a restraint must meet, and then the air bag rule that decides where children should sit. Pay close attention to the ages and the height, because they are easy to blur.

lines.text: Stay in a restraint until four feet nine.

narration.text: Here is the rule for slightly older children. Children aged five to eight must stay in a child restraint system until they are at least four feet nine inches tall. The manual compares the two age groups directly. Under five a child restraint is always required, but from five to eight the restraint is required only until the child reaches four feet nine inches. So for a child under five you never ask about height, and for a child from five to eight you do. Height is the only test the manual gives for ending the restraint between five and eight.

lines.text: More than one child under eight.
Secure as many as reasonably fit.

narration.text: Sometimes a car carries more children than it has room for restraints. A driver carrying more than one child under eight must secure as many of them in child restraints as is reasonable for the size of the passenger area and the number of passengers. The manual repeats the point in plain terms. With several children under eight, the rule is to secure as many as reasonably fit given the passenger area and passenger count, rather than a fixed number of seats. So the driver looks at the space and the passengers and secures as many children in restraints as reasonably fit.

A child restraint must be the right kind and used the right way. Child restraint systems must meet United States Department of Transportation safety standards and be used according to both the seat maker's and the vehicle maker's instructions. Both sets of instructions matter, because the seat and the vehicle each have their own directions for fitting and use. If you ever see a child riding without a restraint, the manual asks for help. The manual asks anyone who sees an unrestrained child in a moving vehicle to report the plate number, city and the child's location to its child-safety hotline.

Here is the trap. When a child no longer needs a car seat, parents sometimes move the child to the front. Air bags save lives but are unsafe for children under twelve, and children twelve and under should never ride in the front seat. The manual sets the two ages side by side. Car-seat ages stop at eight, but the front-seat warning reaches higher: children twelve and under should never ride in front because air bags are unsafe for them. So a nine year old or an eleven year old who no longer needs a car seat should still ride in the back seat.

title.text: If a child rides in front

lines.text: Turn off the passenger air bag.
Most newer vehicles have a switch.
More help from highway safety office.

narration.text: Sometimes there is no choice but to put a child in front. If a child must ride in front, turn off the passenger-side air bag, which most newer vehicles allow with an on or off switch. Use that only when a child truly must ride in front, because the general rule is that children twelve and under ride in back. For more safety information, the manual names a contact. The Arizona Governor's Office of Highway Safety is the contact for more information on safety issues, online at azgohs.gov. That switch is the step the manual gives for this situation.

Here is a quick check: a six year old has reached four feet ten inches. Does Arizona still require a child restraint for that child? No. From five to eight the restraint is required only until the child is at least four feet nine inches tall. Under five a child restraint is always required, but from five to eight the restraint is required only until the child reaches four feet nine inches. If the child were under five, the answer would be different, because a restraint is always required under five. Height decides it at that age.

lines.text: Five to eight: until four feet nine.

narration.text: To close, Arizona law forbids driving on state highways with a child under five who is not properly secured in a child restraint, and children five to eight stay in a restraint until they reach four feet nine inches. With several children under eight, secure as many as reasonably fit. Restraints must meet federal standards and follow both makers' instructions. Children twelve and under should never ride in front because air bags are unsafe for them, and if a child must ride in front, turn off the passenger-side air bag.

why_how.text: Free, round-the-clock travel information helps you check traffic, closures and work zones before a trip.
Knowing the two ways to move through the menus gets you to the report you need.

scenario.text: Rosa is driving to an airport during a busy holiday week.

reasoning.text: She dials five-one-one before leaving and hears current traffic reports and road closures.

result.text: Later she checks the travel website, and neither service costs her anything.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the travel information line charges for its reports.

correction.text: The five-one-one line and its website are free services from the Arizona Department of Transportation.

prompt.text: During a five-one-one call, how do you switch to touch-tone mode?

rationale.text: Pressing the star key switches to touch-tone mode, or you can use voice prompts after the full introduction.

narration.text: This lesson covers a free tool for checking the road before you go. Dialing five-one-one at any time, day or night, gives up-to-the-minute reports on traffic conditions and road closures, transit and airports. In the next slides we look at the other reports the service offers, how to move through its menus, and where to find the same information online. The first group of reports covers traffic conditions and road closures, and it also includes transit and airports, all updated up to the minute. The line is available every hour of every day.

The five-one-one service also reports on tourism, gives quick reports for the metro regions, and covers construction and work zones. That makes it useful for more than rush-hour traffic. If you are heading into an area with roadwork, or traveling somewhere new, the same call can tell you about work zones and travel conditions along the way, along with the traffic and closure reports from the first slide. So one call can cover traffic, closures, transit, airports, tourism, the metro regions and work zones, depending on what you need for your trip.

Here is a mistaken idea some drivers have: that a service with live reports must charge for them. It does not. Travel information is also online at the five-one-one website, and both the phone line and the website are free services from the Arizona Department of Transportation. Because both are free, checking road conditions before a trip costs nothing but a minute of your time. The website and the phone line both give travel information, so you can choose whichever is easier for you before you set out, and neither one charges for the reports.

Here is how to use the line once you are connected. On a five-one-one call, pressing the star key switches to touch-tone mode, so you choose options with the keypad. If you prefer voice prompts, listen to the whole introduction first and cut down any background noise around you, so the system can understand your choices. Either way, you reach the same reports. The two methods are alternatives: touch-tone uses the keypad after you press the star key, while voice prompts listen for your choices after the full introduction. Cutting background noise is part of the voice method.

lines.text: You are on a five-one-one call.
How do you switch to touch-tone?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: during a five-one-one call, how do you switch to touch-tone mode? The answer is to press the star key. If you would rather use voice prompts, the manual says to listen to the whole introduction and cut background noise. Both options lead to the same free travel reports, including traffic, closures and work zones. So there are two ways to move through the menus. Press the star key to use the keypad, or listen through the whole introduction and cut background noise to use voice prompts. Knowing both lets you pick whichever works for you.

lines.text: Traffic, closures, transit, airports, work zones.

narration.text: To finish, dialing five-one-one at any time gives current reports on traffic conditions, road closures, transit and airports, plus tourism, metro-region quick reports, and construction and work zones. Press the star key for touch-tone mode, or use voice prompts by listening to the whole introduction and cutting background noise. The same travel information is on the five-one-one website, and both the line and the website are free services from the Arizona Department of Transportation. You can use it any time, day or night.

why_how.text: A well-kept vehicle is safer and cheaper to run, and the law sets firm rules for loads and brakes.

scenario.text: Dev's car fails its required emission inspection at an authorized station.

reasoning.text: He has thirty days to fix the problem and return for a follow-up re-check.

result.text: He follows the owner's manual and has a qualified technician handle the repair.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a motorcycle needs the same two brake systems as a car.

correction.text: Cars and trucks need a foot brake and a parking brake, each on at least two wheels, while a motorcycle needs only one brake worked by hand or foot.

prompt.text: How many brake systems must a car have?

answer.text: Two: a foot brake and a parking brake.

rationale.text: Cars and trucks need both a foot brake and a parking brake, each working on at least two wheels.

narration.text: This lesson covers the driver's duty to keep a vehicle safe. Here is the principle. Drivers are responsible for making sure the vehicle they drive is safe, and an unsafe vehicle costs more to run than a maintained one. And here is the benefit. A vehicle in good condition gives you an extra margin of safety when you need it. From there we look at routine maintenance, what happens when a vehicle fails an emission inspection, the law on loads that can fall or leak, and the brake systems every vehicle must have. Each rule applies to every vehicle you drive.

lines.text: Thirty days after a failed emission test.

narration.text: Maintenance starts with the right guide. Follow the owner's manual for routine maintenance; some tasks you can do yourself, while others need a qualified technician. Emission inspections have their own timeline. If your vehicle fails a required emission inspection at an authorized station, you get thirty days to fix the problem and return for a follow-up emission re-check. The manual sums that up as a single window. A failed emission inspection opens a thirty-day window to fix the problem and come back for a follow-up re-check.

lines.text: No load may drop or sift.
No load may leak or escape.

narration.text: Arizona law bars driving or moving a vehicle on a road unless it is built or loaded so none of its load can drop, sift, leak or otherwise escape. The manual stresses how wide the rule is. The secured-load rule applies to any vehicle on a highway, street or roadway, and covers loads that drop, sift or leak as well as any other way a load can escape. So a load of loose material, a leaking container or anything that could fall is covered, whatever the vehicle and whatever the road. Securing a load is part of keeping your vehicle safe.

lines.text: Good working brakes on every vehicle.
A foot brake and a parking brake.
Each on at least two wheels.

narration.text: Brakes have specific requirements. Every motor vehicle must have brakes in good working condition, and cars and trucks need both a foot brake and a parking brake. Each set of brakes on a car or truck must work on at least two wheels, and a motorcycle needs at least one brake applied by hand or foot. So a car or truck has two separate brake systems, and each of them must work on at least two wheels. Picture a car with a foot brake for stopping and a parking brake as the second system, each acting on at least two wheels. If either system is missing, the car does not meet the rule.

Here is the trap. People sometimes apply the car brake rule to motorcycles. The manual separates them. Cars and trucks need two separate brake systems, a foot brake and a parking brake, each acting on at least two wheels, while a motorcycle needs only one brake worked by hand or foot. So a question that asks about a motorcycle's minimum brakes is looking for one brake worked by hand or foot, while a question about a car or truck is looking for two systems on at least two wheels each. Read the vehicle type in each question first.

Here is a quick check: how many brake systems must a car have? The answer is two, a foot brake and a parking brake. Every motor vehicle must have brakes in good working condition, and cars and trucks need both a foot brake and a parking brake. Each set must also work on at least two wheels. If you said one, you were thinking of the motorcycle minimum. Cars and trucks need two separate brake systems, a foot brake and a parking brake, each acting on at least two wheels, while a motorcycle needs only one brake worked by hand or foot.

lines.text: Thirty days after a failed emission test.
Secured loads and two brake systems.

narration.text: To sum up, drivers are responsible for making sure their vehicle is safe, and a well-kept vehicle gives an extra margin of safety and costs less to run. Follow the owner's manual for maintenance. A failed emission inspection gives you thirty days to fix the problem and return for a re-check. No load may drop, sift, leak or otherwise escape. Every motor vehicle needs good brakes: cars and trucks need a foot brake and a parking brake, each on at least two wheels, and a motorcycle needs at least one brake. Keep each rule in mind as you prepare.
